groups.label: Moral Ideals and Truth in Soul
groups.summary: Commentary on the early books examines the defense of justice as an ennobling ideal independent of external circumstances, alongside the distinction between medicinal fictions and the corrupting lie in the soul.
groups.rationale: Both entries derive from early commentary (Book II) dealing with foundational moral abstractions: defining the intrinsic value of justice and distinguishing true inner deception from practical verbal fictions.

groups.label: Dialectic and the Cave Rulers
groups.summary: These passages address the philosophical education culminating in dialectic as the coping-stone of sciences, the nature of abstract thinking, and the dual disorders of eyesight faced when compelling enlightened philosophers to descend into the cave to govern.
groups.rationale: A tightly clustered set of commentary entries around Book VII covering dialectic, mathematical abstraction, and the allegorical descent and optical disorientation of philosopher-rulers.

groups.label: Constitutional and Moral Decay
groups.summary: Socrates and the commentator outline the four degenerate forms of government—timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny—and their corresponding human types, tracking an ethical gradation from reason down to a tyrannical monster passion.
groups.rationale: Consecutive commentary entries focused specifically on Book VIII's sequential decline of political regimes and individual ethical characters.

groups.label: Pleasure, Soul, and City Pattern
groups.summary: Discussions analyze the tripartite soul using the image of the man, lion, and many-headed beast, establish the rational hierarchy of pleasures, and present the ideal city as an internal celestial pattern for individual self-governance.
groups.rationale: These entries form a coherent thematic and spatial group from the Book IX commentary evaluating the psychological harmony, superior pleasures of reason, and the heavenly model of justice.

groups.label: Ideals, Poetry, and Statesmanship
groups.summary: Commentary addresses Plato's rejection of imitative poetry in favor of universals, the nature of the ideal Republic as an unattainable vision rather than an earthly reality, the practical tensions of the philosopher-statesman, and modern dual ideals reconciled through faith.
groups.rationale: A sequence of broader synthetic commentary reflections exploring the gulf between speculative philosophical ideals (statecraft, poetry critique, and modern religious/historical progress) and empirical reality.

groups.label: Virtue, Harm, and Happiness
groups.summary: In Book I dialogue, Socrates argues that justice can never involve harming others and demonstrates that because a just soul lives well, the just person is inherently happy and profitable while the unjust person is miserable.
groups.rationale: These three items represent direct Socratic dialogue from Book I establishing Socrates' early refutations and core claims regarding harm, virtue, and the inherent profitability of justice.
